design_rationale: The study is described as a prospective, randomized, single-blinded clinical trial in which subjects were randomly assigned to one of four treatment groups using a random number generator with block design.
Participants were randomly allocated to exercise therapy or usual care using a computer-generated list stratified by age and recruiting physician with block randomization.

domain_judgments.rationale: The allocation sequence was computer-generated by an independent researcher, stratified with block randomization, ensuring concealed allocation, and baseline characteristics were well balanced between groups.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The randomisation was done by an independent researcher who used a computer generated list in which patients were stratified by age (14-17 years or 18 years and older) and by recruiting physician (GP or sport physician). A block size of eight was used within the four strata.

domain_judgments.rationale: Although blinding was impossible due to the nature of exercise therapy, the primary analysis followed an intention-to-treat approach and deviations/cross-overs (e.g. control patients seeking physical therapy) reflected trial context without biasing results in favour of the intervention.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Differences between the intervention and control group were analysed on an intention to treat basis. Subgroup analysis was performed for predefined subgroups based on age and type of recruiting physician.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data were available for a high proportion of participants at both 3 months (122/131, ~93%) and 12 months (117/131, ~89%), with balanced and low loss to follow-up across arms.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Between 3 and 12 months, another eight patients were lost to follow-up (five in the intervention group and three in the control group; see fig 1). One person who was lost before the 3 month follow-up was located and available for follow-up in the 3-12 month period.

domain_judgments.rationale: The outcomes (pain numerical rating scale, Kujala score, and self-reported recovery) are patient-reported subjective measures assessed in an open-label trial where participants were aware of their intervention group assignment, introducing potential reporting bias.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A methodological problem that cannot be solved in randomised controlled trials of exercise therapy is that patients in the intervention group cannot be blinded for the exercise therapy and, therefore, may be biased for positive outcome (placebo effect).

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was prospectively registered, an a priori protocol was published, and all pre-specified primary outcomes and analyses were reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The study protocol has been published previously.13 ... Trial registration ISRCTN83938749.

overall_summary: The study was well-conducted with robust randomization, intention-to-treat analysis, low attrition, and an a priori published protocol. However, because it was an open-label trial with subjective, participant-reported outcomes (pain, function, and recovery), there are some concerns regarding risk of bias in the measurement of outcomes.

design_rationale: The authors explicitly describe random allocation of participants into three groups using sealed opaque envelopes picked by an individual not involved in the study.

domain_judgments.rationale: Allocation concealment was ensured with sealed opaque envelopes chosen by an independent individual, and baseline characteristics were balanced across groups.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The assignment of patients in the 3 groups was performed randomly using opaque and sealed envelopes containing the names of the groups: CO, KE, and KHE. The envelopes were picked by an individual not involved in this study.

domain_judgments.rationale: Although participants and physical therapists could not be blinded given the nature of the exercise interventions, protocols were strictly supervised with high adherence and an intention-to-treat analysis showed consistent findings.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: We performed an intention-to-treat analysis, and the results were consistent with the per-protocol analysis as presented above.

domain_judgments.rationale: Dropout was very low (4 out of 70 patients, ~5.7%), reasons/numbers were balanced across active groups, and results remained consistent under an ITT analysis.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Two patients in the KE group and 2 patients in the KHE group did not complete the study.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome measures were validated scales and physical performance tests assessed by an independent examiner masked to group allocation.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: After the inclusion of the participants, a single examiner was responsible for the administration of all tests and questionnaires performed before and after the intervention. This examiner was blind to the group assignment of the patients and did not participate in the intervention.

domain_judgments.rationale: All pre-specified outcome measures outlined in the methods are thoroughly reported with means, standard deviations, and confidence intervals without evidence of selective outcome reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The data for the 2 functional scales (AKPS and LEFS), the singlelimb single hop test, and the NPRS were analyzed using separate 3-by-2 (group by time) mixed-model 2-way ANOVAs.

overall_summary: The trial utilized concealed random allocation, blinded outcome assessment, had minimal attrition (<6%), and reported all intended outcomes with both per-protocol and intention-to-treat analyses, resulting in an overall low risk of bias.

design_rationale: The study explicitly states that participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups using sealed and numbered envelopes.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and exercise supervising physical therapists could not be blinded to the exercise interventions versus control, which could potentially introduce performance bias or deviations from the intended protocol.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The patients in the control group participated only in the testing procedures, and all participants were asked to avoid sports or other painprovocative activities during the exercise intervention period but to participate in their standard army (clerical and administration) duties.

domain_judgments.rationale: Although sealed and numbered envelopes were used for allocation concealment, the specific method of random sequence generation was not reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Patients were then randomly assigned by opening a sealed and numbered envelope to 1 of 3 groups: a control group (n = 15), the SJNWBE group (n = 15), and the MJWBE group (n = 15).

domain_judgments.rationale: All randomized participants completed the study and had complete outcome data available for analysis.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: All 45 participants completed the study.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome assessment was conducted by an independent assessor who was blinded to group allocation, and objective/standardized measurement instruments were utilized.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Testing was conducted by an independent assessor (an experienced physical therapist) blinded to intervention group.

domain_judgments.rationale: There is no mention of a pre-registered trial protocol or pre-specified statistical analysis plan to ensure reported outcomes were not selectively chosen.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) (group, 3 levels; time, 2 levels) was used to compare the baseline results with the 6-week assessments across the 3 groups for each of the outcome measures.

overall_summary: The study is rated as having some concerns overall due to lack of detail regarding the random sequence generation method, lack of participant/provider blinding given an unblinded exercise intervention, and absence of a pre-registered protocol.

design_rationale: The study is described as a randomized controlled trial where participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups (LPHA, LP, or control) in blocks of 9 using numbered opaque envelopes.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants were randomized using block randomization with allocation concealment via numbered opaque envelopes, and baseline characteristics were comparable across groups.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Participants were randomly assigned to the LP group, LPHA group, or control group in blocks of 9 (chosen through numbered opaque envelopes)... There were no significant between-group differences for any of the demographic variables.

domain_judgments.rationale: Interventions were administered consistently according to protocol by a therapist unaware of the study aims, participant compliance was high, and an intention-to-treat analysis was performed.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A single physical therapist, unaware of the purpose of the study, was responsible for randomization and interventions... Data were subjected to an intention-to-treat analysis and included all dropouts.

domain_judgments.rationale: Attrition was relatively low (11%), balanced across groups, reasons for dropout were unrelated to the trial outcome or knee pain, and intention-to-treat analysis including all dropouts was conducted.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Ten participants later dropped out of the study due to personal factors (not knee pain) or work commitment. Seventy-nine participants completed the trial (27 in each exercise group and 25 in the control group, Fig. 1)... Data were subjected to an intention-to-treat analysis and included all dropouts.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome assessors were blinded to group allocation, and validated outcome measures (VAS, Lysholm scale, and standardized ultrasonography) were applied consistently across all groups.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Two assessment sessions were performed by another physical therapist (blinded to each patient’s grouping) before and after the 8-week intervention.

domain_judgments.rationale: All prespecified outcomes including pain (VAS-W), knee function (Lysholm scale), and ultrasound-measured VMO morphology (CSA and volume) were fully analyzed and reported according to the predefined analysis plan.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The purpose of this study was to investigate the surplus effect of hip adduction to seated LP exercise on VMO morphology, pain, and function in patients with PFPS. We hypothesized that incorporation of hip adduction with leg-press training (LPHA) would result in morebeneficial effects on VMO hypertrophy, pain, and functional improvement compared with LP training alone.

overall_summary: The study was judged to be at low risk of bias across all RoB 2 domains. Concealed randomization, blinded outcome assessment, low and balanced attrition analyzed with intention-to-treat methods, and comprehensive reporting of predefined outcomes support an overall low risk of bias.

design_rationale: The study is described as an 'observer blind, prospective, factorial design randomised controlled trial' where participants were randomly allocated using a computer-generated program.

domain_judgments.rationale: Although a computer-generated randomization programme was used, no details are provided regarding allocation concealment, and allocation was conducted directly by the physiotherapist.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The patients were then randomly allocated by the physiotherapist to one of four groups using an individualised computer generated randomisation programme.

domain_judgments.rationale: Given the nature of physical therapy, blinding of patients was not possible, but treatment contact time was balanced across arms and analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The patients themselves were not completely blinded because they were aware that of the four types of treatment one group would receive advice only... Patients who failed to attend were included in the analysis on an intention to treat basis.

domain_judgments.rationale: While 3-month primary outcome data appear complete or analyzed via ITT, follow-up at 12 months had substantial loss to follow-up (32 of 81 patients, ~40% missing).
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: 10 patients withdrew during the study and these were included in the analysis on an intention to treat basis. 49 patients returned the questionnaires at 12 months.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome assessments at the end of the intervention were conducted by an independent observer who was blinded to group assignment.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A blinded independent observer undertook assessment on the sixth visit. The primary outcome measure was an assessment of patient satisfaction (satisfied = discharge, not satisfied = continue physiotherapy, or refer to consultant).

domain_judgments.rationale: There is no trial registration or published pre-specified protocol mentioned, raising some concerns for selective reporting across multiple timepoints and analyses.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The primary outcome measure was an assessment of patient satisfaction (satisfied = discharge, not satisfied = continue physiotherapy, or refer to consultant). Secondary outcome measures were a visual analogue pain score...

overall_summary: The trial has some concerns regarding risk of bias overall due to an unclear method of allocation concealment, substantial missing data at 12-month follow-up, and lack of a pre-registered statistical analysis plan.
